headers.description: Optional headers to send with the request as a dictionary of header values.

Content-Type.description: The media type of the resource being requested, typically 'application/json'.

Authorization.description: The credentials to authenticate a user agent with a server, typically formatted as 'Bearer {token}'.

timeout.description: The maximum amount of time to wait for a response from the server, in seconds. A longer timeout may be necessary for slower network connections or overloaded servers. This is a float type value.

params.description: URL parameters to append to the URL. Sent as a dictionary of key-value pairs.

query.description: The query parameter for search or filtering.

page.description: The page number parameter for pagination. Used to retrieve a specific page of results.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials formatted as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem), if required for the request.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names and values.

sessionid.description: Session identifier cookie, used to recognize client sessions on the server.

csrftoken.description: CSRF protection token cookie, used to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary, mapping protocol or protocol and hostname to the URL of the proxy.

http.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTP requests, including the port number.

https.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTPS requests, including the port number.

stream.description: Whether to stream the download of the response. If False, the response content will be immediately downloaded. Streaming is useful for handling large files or responses.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not. Set to False to skip certificate verification, which is not recommended unless you are sure of the server's identity.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑reference guide to the most popular public APIs that accept an IP address and return business‑oriented data (company name, domain, contact details, etc.). All of them expose a simple HTTP GET endpoint, usually require an API key, and return JSON. I’ve grouped them by the type of data they provide and added a short “how‑to” snippet so you can test one right away. | # | Service | What it gives you | Typical endpoint | Pricing (as of 2026‑06) | Quick test (Python) | |---|---------|-------------------|------------------|------------------------|---------------------| | 1 | **ipinfo.io** | Company name, domain, industry, logo, contact email, phone, address, etc. | `https://ipinfo.io//json` | Free tier: 50k req/month, paid plans start at $5/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://ipinfo.io/8.8.8.8/json', params={'token': 'YOUR_TOKEN'})
print(r.json())``` | | 2 | **ipstack.com** | Company name, domain, contact email, phone, address, industry, logo, etc. | `https://api.ipstack.com/?access_key=YOUR_KEY` | Free tier: 10k req/month, paid plans start at $10/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://api.ipstack.com/8.8.8.8', params={'access_key': 'YOUR_KEY'})
print(r.json())``` | | 3 | **ipapi.co** | Company name, domain, contact email, phone, address, industry, logo, etc. | `https://ipapi.co//json/` | Free tier: 30k req/month, paid plans start at $9/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://ipapi.co/8.8.8.8/json/')
print(r.json())``` | | 4 | **ipgeolocation.io** | Company name, domain, contact email, phone, address, industry, logo, etc. | `https://api.ipgeolocation.io/ipgeo?apiKey=YOUR_KEY&ip=8.8.8.8` | Free tier: 15k req/month, paid plans start at $7/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://api.ipgeolocation.io/ipgeo', params={'apiKey':'YOUR_KEY','ip':'8.8.8.8'})
print(r.json())``` | | 5 | **ipwhois.io** | Company name, domain, contact email, phone, address, industry, logo, etc. | `https://ipwhois.app/json/` | Free tier: 10k req/month, paid plans start at $5/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://ipwhois.app/json/8.8.8.8')
print(r.json())``` | | 6 | **ipdata.co** | Company name, domain, contact email, phone, address, industry, logo, etc. | `https://api.ipdata.co/?api-key=YOUR_KEY` | Free tier: 25k req/month, paid plans start at $9/mo | ```python
import requests
r = requests.get('https://api.ipdata.co/8.8.8.8', params={'api-key':'YOUR_KEY'})
print(r.json())``` | | 7 | **ipinfo.io + WhoisXML API** | Combines IP geolocation with WHOIS lookup for domain/company data. | `https://ipinfo.io//json` + `https://www.whoisxmlapi.com/whoisserver/WhoisService?apiKey=YOUR_KEY&domainName=example.com` | WHOISXML API: free tier 5000 req/month, paid plans start at $19/mo | See example below. | --- ## How to get started 1. **Pick a provider** – If you only need basic company info, `ipinfo.io` or `ipapi.co` are great starters. 2. **Sign up** – Create an account on the provider’s website and grab your API key/token. 3. **Make a request** – Use the snippet above (replace `YOUR_KEY` or `YOUR_TOKEN`) and hit the endpoint. 4. **Parse the JSON** – The response will contain fields like `company`, `domain`, `email`, `phone`, `address`, `industry`, `logo`, etc. ### Example: Using `ipinfo.io` to get company data ```python import requests IP = "8.8.8.8" # Replace with the IP you want to look up TOKEN = "YOUR_TOKEN" # Your ipinfo.io API token url = f"https://ipinfo.io/{IP}/json" params = {"token": TOKEN} response = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=5) data = response.json() print("Company:", data.get("company", "N/A")) print("Domain:", data.get("domain", "N/A")) print("Email:", data.get("email", "N/A")) print("Phone:", data.get("phone", "N/A")) print("Address:", data.get("address", "N/A")) print("Industry:", data.get("industry", "N/A")) print("Logo:", data.get("logo", "N/A")) ``` > **Tip:** Many of these services also expose a *reverse DNS* lookup that can give you the hostname associated with the IP, which you can then feed into a WHOIS API for even richer company data. --- ## Combining IP lookup with WHOIS for deeper data If you need the company’s official domain and want to pull the official contact details from the domain’s WHOIS record, you can chain two calls: ```python import requests IP = "8.8.8.8" IPINFO_TOKEN = "YOUR_IPINFO_TOKEN" WHOISXML_KEY = "YOUR_WHOISXML_KEY" # 1. Get the domain from the IP ipinfo_url = f"https://ipinfo.io/{IP}/json" ipinfo_resp = requests.get(ipinfo_url, params={"token": IPINFO_TOKEN}) ipinfo_data = ipinfo_resp.json() domain = ipinfo_data.get("domain") if domain: # 2. Query WHOIS for that domain whois_url = "https://www.whoisxmlapi.com/whoisserver/WhoisService" whois_params = { "apiKey": WHOISXML_KEY, "domainName": domain, "outputFormat": "JSON" } whois_resp = requests.get(whois_url, params=whois_params) whois_data = whois_resp.json() # Extract contact info registrant = whois_data.get("WhoisRecord", {}).get("registrant", {}) print("Registrant Name:", registrant.get("name")) print("Registrant Email:", registrant.get("email")) print("Registrant Phone:", registrant.get("phone")) else: print("No domain found for IP.") ``` --- ## Things to keep in mind | Issue | Recommendation | |-------|----------------| | **Rate limits** | All free tiers have limits (10k–50k requests/month). If you need higher volume, consider a paid plan or a dedicated IP‑lookup service. | | **Accuracy** | Company data is often derived from WHOIS, reverse DNS, or public registries. It may be incomplete or outdated. | | **Privacy** | Some jurisdictions restrict the disclosure of contact info. Make sure you comply with GDPR, CCPA, etc. | | **Caching** | IP addresses rarely change company ownership. Cache responses for at least 24–48 h to reduce API calls. | | **Error handling** | Always check for HTTP status codes and JSON errors (`"error"` field). | --- ### Bottom line - **Fastest, easiest**: `ipinfo.io` or `ipapi.co` – single endpoint, rich JSON. - **Deepest data**: Combine an IP lookup with a WHOIS API (e.g., `whoisxmlapi.com`). - **Cost‑effective**: Most providers offer a generous free tier; upgrade only if you hit the limit. Happy hunting! If you need help wiring this into your stack (Node.js, Go, etc.) just let me know.
